Series and seasons follow the same rule: the server records a new season's premiere as soon as its date has begun in the earliest time zone (UTC+14) and refreshes the series then, so New Season appears at your own midnight even east of UTC, and not before it west of UTC. Added dates (Just Added) are exact times. Dates read Tomorrow, then a localized weekday for two to five days ahead, then a localized short date such as Nov 6. The user's Jellyfin display language is preferred, followed by the JE language and browser locale.

With Compact density, Season Premiere becomes Premiere; Season Finale and Series Finale become Finale; Complete Season becomes Complete; Airing Today becomes Today; Coming Soon becomes Soon; Just Added becomes Added; New Episode becomes New Ep; Leaving in 5d becomes 5d left; Won't direct play becomes Remux. Other labels retain their full text.

docs.title: Scenes
docs.text:
Administrator native-poster preview using cached Jellyfin streams and TMDB keywords; not a physical-client capture.

On Media Tags → Status badges, Scenes enables Post-credits and Mid-credits for movies. It starts off for both administrators and users. An administrator must enable the family on the Media Tags admin tab’s Status badges tab and configure the existing TMDB key. Then users can enable Scenes for their account. The movie in both the personal and admin live previews carries a Post-credits sample, shown when Scenes is enabled and no higher-priority family is selected.

TMDB’s exact aftercreditsstinger and duringcreditsstinger keywords supply the facts. The server resolves them daily through its shared response cache and keeps the result in the tag cache; no browser or native poster request contacts TMDB per card. A failed lookup omits an unknown marker and keeps previously confirmed facts for later retry. No keyword is not a guarantee that a movie has no extra scene. Scenes follows the usual one-badge priority, after Just Added; Post-credits wins when both keywords exist. Native posters and the batch fallback use the same facts and switches.

docs.title: TMDB and trending
docs.text:
A TMDB API key is required for Airing Today, Airs, Returns, Season Finale, Series Finale and Complete Season. Without one, Jellyfin supplies added/release badges, New Season, Season Premiere and Returning/Ended. Cancelled requires TMDB. No Seerr schedule fallback is used.

Trending reads #N Today from TMDB's daily list when a key is configured. Without a key, or when TMDB fails or returns no rankable titles, it reads #N This Week from Seerr. With neither source, no rank appears. Only movies and series with TMDB IDs receive ranks.

The server shares up to 60 movie/series ranks for 30 minutes, with a five-minute retry after an empty answer. The list contains only public TMDB IDs and ranks. Changed ranks re-badge cards already on the page.

For series cards on screen, and parent series of season/episode cards, the browser batches up to 50 accessible IDs through GET /JellyfinEnhanced/status-tags/series. It retains schedules for an hour and retries failures after five minutes. The server shares TMDB responses for six hours, with at most four lookups in flight and 35 upstream requests per ten-second window. If the series response omits episode_type, its latest aired season supplies it. For an ended series whose latest episode is a special, the newest aired regular season also supplies a separate last regular episode. Parent aggregates fetched through /tag-data are shared by series and episode cards, expire after ten minutes, and are discarded on user or filter changes. No schedule is stored per user or in the tag cache. One shared viewport observer gates schedule requests; offscreen, detached and recycled cards do not dispatch lookups. Targets are released on removal, identity reuse, renderer cleanup and user change. A single timer re-evaluates labels at the next local midnight, and visibility/focus events refresh active cards after a suspended tab returns. User changes, renderer cleanup and pagehide cancel midnight, batch and retry timers; initialisation and pageshow resume them.

docs.title: Leaving soon (Maintainerr)
docs.text:
Maintainerr puts the media its rules will delete into collections (often one called Leaving Soon) and deletes each item a set number of days after it was added. With Leaving soon on, cards say when an item goes.

An administrator sets the source in *arr › Maintainerr (shown as a linked copy under Services; the Media Tags › Status badges › Leaving soon section shows its live state, with a Refresh now button and a link to the settings, and the Overview tab's Service Status lists Maintainerr with its last read):

Setting Default What it does Maintainerr URL Empty The address this server reaches Maintainerr at (http:// or https://, no credentials or query). The server reads GET /api/collections and computes each item's delete date from addDate + deleteAfterDays. Inactive collections are skipped. Redirects are not followed: use the final address (a redirect shows as the last failure and is logged with its host) Maintainerr API key Empty Sent as X-Api-Key when set. It is kept in the plugin configuration like the other keys and never sent to users or written to the Leaving soon snapshot or logs Leaving collections Empty Existing Jellyfin collection names, one per line (up to 20), whose members count as leaving, without a date. For setups without the API; nothing is created Refresh every 6 hours How often the server reads the source again (1–168 hours) Mark, keep and postpone from the item menu On Administrators get Mark for removal, Keep (cancel removal) and Postpone removal in an item's ⋮ menu (see below). Needs the Maintainerr URL Leaving soon home row On A Leaving soon row on a Home Screen Sections home page (see below). Needs the Maintainerr URL Leaving soon (family switch) Off Whether new users start with the badge on

Cards never ask Maintainerr: the Refresh Leaving Soon Tags scheduled task (hourly, acting only once the interval has passed), a source change and Refresh now (in the Services card and in the Leaving soon section) read it on the server and put the result into the tag cache entries (Leaving). A failed request (including an answer that lists entries but no collection or member it can read) keeps the last good answer and retries after 15 minutes, then 30, 60 and so on, at most the refresh interval; the card shows the last read, the next one, the item counts and the last failure. Maintainerr items are matched by their Jellyfin item id (mediaServerId); a Plex-backed Maintainerr's movies and shows are matched by TMDB id. A season or episode leaves with its season or series, whichever goes first. Users who can see an item see its Maintainerr badge; a badge that only a leaving collection gives is shown to users who can access that collection (as for collection-matched Custom Tags). The collection names and the Maintainerr address stay on the server.

LeavingSoonMaintainerrApiKey is explicitly excluded from both user and administrator portable exports/imports, public/private configuration and runtime snapshots. The Services card keeps the key in a password field saved with the configuration page's Save button, like the other service keys. The administrator-only core Jellyfin plugin configuration API retains its normal credential-editing contract. Source URLs, collection names and cadence are administrator settings; private collection provenance never reaches tag clients.

docs.title: Marking, keeping and postponing from the item menu
docs.text:
With Mark, keep and postpone from the item menu on (and a Maintainerr URL), an administrator's ⋮ menu on a movie or series (the detail page's or a card's) gets:

Item Row What happens Not in Maintainerr Mark for removal The item is added to Maintainerr's manual collection for its library, at once, and a toast with Undo follows (Undo removes it again). There is no confirm dialog In Maintainerr Keep (cancel removal) The item is removed from its Maintainerr collection; the toast's Undo marks it again In Maintainerr Postpone removal A small chooser: +7, +14, +30 or +90 days, a custom count (1–3650), or Reset timer (count the collection's days from today)

Maintainerr is set up first, as today, with a rule per library that uses a manual collection (its "Use manual collection" option); the plugin never creates collections. An item is matched to the one active manual collection of its type (movie or show) on its Jellyfin library. When one library has several (say a 4K and an HD list, each tied to its own Radarr), the plugin asks each collection's Radarr or Sonarr server, as Maintainerr lists them, whether it holds the item (by TMDB id for movies, TVDB id for series) and uses the one that does. When nothing fits, or more than one does, the toast says so and names Maintainerr's collections. Every change reads Maintainerr again at once, so the badge, the row and the next menu follow without waiting for the scheduled refresh. The rows are only offered to administrators, and the server refuses everyone else regardless; the Maintainerr address and key, and the *arr addresses and keys Maintainerr holds, never reach the browser. Seasons and episodes get no rows.

The rows are added to Jellyfin's item menu the same way as Media Tags, so they share its dependence on jellyfin-web's private menu behaviour (see One item's look).

docs.title: The Leaving soon home row
docs.text: With Leaving soon home row on (and a Maintainerr URL), the plugin registers a Leaving soon section with the Home Screen Sections plugin when that plugin is installed (it also needs File Transformation to draw its rows). The row lists Maintainerr's items the viewer can see, soonest removal first, movies and series only (a leaving season or episode shows as its series), up to 20. It is registered on every start (Home Screen Sections keeps registrations in memory) and, if Home Screen Sections has no entry for it yet, added to its section list enabled for everyone with user override allowed; users who keep their own section list may need to turn it on there. The Leaving soon section of the Media Tags tab says whether the row is registered, or which plugin is missing. The cards carry the usual Leaving soon badge for users who have it on.

docs.title: Direct-play warning
docs.text:
With Direct-play warning on, movies and episodes that this browser would not play as they are get Transcode (video, audio, subtitles, bitrate or HDR need converting) or Won't direct play (only the container needs a remux). Hover the badge for the reasons, for example Transcode: video codec hevc, audio codec dts.

The answer comes from Jellyfin's own negotiation, POST /Items/{id}/PlaybackInfo with the device profile the web player itself would send: a port of jellyfin-web 12.1's browser profile (the same browser checks for containers, codecs, HDR, interlacing and levels, and your Playback settings in this browser such as DTS, TrueHD, subtitle burn-in and PGS rendering, audio channels and maximum resolution), or the app's own profile in a desktop or TV app, and your saved video quality for this network (the one you chose, or the last automatic measurement). Signing in as another user or changing one of these settings in the page builds the profile again, so lookups ask with the new one. Nothing plays or transcodes. Lookups run only for cards on screen that show no other status badge, in idle moments, at most two at a time (also across page changes and user switches: a request still on its way keeps its place until it ends, at most 15 seconds, after which it is cancelled and counts as a failed lookup) and a few per idle slice. An item with several versions is asked about the version its card shows: the one you picked on its details page (Quality Tags remember it in this browser), else the one Jellyfin plays by default. Answers are kept per item, version, device profile and quality for a day, in memory and in this browser's tag cache store, and only for the media they were given for (each version's revision from the server, covering every fact a playback profile can check: bitrate, bit depth, level, scan type, frame rate, codec tag, anamorphic, reference frames, rotation, NAL length size, colour primaries, space and range, HDR10+ and Dolby Vision facts, and the codec, language and external, default and forced flags of every stream, subtitles included; a card without that revision fingerprints the same list from the facts it holds): a replaced or re-encoded file is asked about again at once, an answer stored before this check existed is asked again, and an answer still on its way for the old file is never shown for the new one; a failed lookup is retried after ten minutes. It skips every item Jellyfin would probe to answer: a .strm item (Jellyfin refreshes it with a remote probe on each such lookup, even when it was probed before) and an item whose tag data lists streams but no video stream in its first media source (media never probed) are not looked up and show no warning. Items whose tag data lists no streams at all (stripped or not sent) are looked up. It is a per-browser check: another device can play the same file differently. Native Poster Tags never show it, because a static poster has no client profile.

Native status badges

Native Poster Tags draw the same winning status chip, with your family switches and the administrator's day windows. Native trending follows the web's sources and wording: TMDB's daily list (#N Today), else Seerr's weekly list (#N This Week), refreshed every 30 minutes (5 after an empty answer) in the background; with neither source it shows no popular badge. A poster request never waits for either. Native schedule facts share the six-hour TMDB response cache. Native posters show Leaving soon like the web (dates in the time zone saved with your web settings) but never the direct-play warning.

Cache, access filtering and styling

The current tag cache schema (CurrentCacheSchemaVersion in Services/TagCacheService.cs) includes Leaving (DeleteAt, Unix ms or null), Awards, Logos, CustomTags, named-source Ratings, LibraryId (library rules), Status, LatestEpisodeAired, LatestEpisodeIndex (Season, Episode, IsLast), SeasonPremiere (Season, Aired), SeasonAddedSpan (First, Last, Count) and EpisodeIndex (Season, Episode, nullable IsLast). Dates are Unix milliseconds UTC. Movie, series and episode entries can have PremiereDate. The persisted browser copy is replaced when its entry schema differs.

All derived episode facts follow the existing access-filtering and filterRevision path. When any contributing episode is inaccessible, related aggregates are omitted conservatively; the shared entry is unchanged. The server-only StatusEpisodeIds, LatestEpisodeId and NextEpisodePremiere never enter client responses. NextEpisodePremiere records the next relevant future air date; reconciliation and snapshot load recompute elapsed boundaries without requiring a metadata save. Compatible snapshots without the optional field seed the boundary from their cached episode dates. Episode changes refresh sibling indexes and contributor lists together. With server cache off, tag-data?latestEpisode=true computes through the target user's access.

Spoiler Guard preserves added-date badges and movie/series trending ranks. Guarded season/episode entries omit air dates and milestone indexes, suppressing premiere/finale badges. Complete Season still needs the whole season among their visible episodes.

Style .status-tag or its --trending, --new, --added, --schedule, --milestone, --status, --leaving, --playback modifiers. Each chip has data-je-status: existing styles keep added, newMovie, newSeries, newEpisode and trending; new badges use keys such as new_season, every Leaving soon badge uses leaving and both direct-play warnings direct_play (which also carries data-je-dp and a tooltip); the number inside a trending chip is .status-tag-rank.

docs.title: Awards Tags
docs.text:
Awards adds IMDb Top 250, Rotten Tomatoes Certified Fresh, Oscar Winner, Emmy Winner and Letterboxd Top 250 chips to movie and series posters. Each has a source logo. Hover for its list rank or most recent known ceremony year. Clicking a chip opens the poster’s item; modifier and middle clicks open it in a new tab. Chips add no keyboard tab stops. In Summary, the hidden summary pill lets pointer events reach the revealed chips even when its three facts come from other groups. A nomination never produces a winner chip, and a high tomato score never implies Certified Fresh.

Fixture facts demonstrate all ribbons without an MDBList key; this is rendering evidence, not verified award history for these titles.

How to use:

  1. An administrator enables Media Tags settings → Groups → Awards, then selects the ribbons. Each edit saves automatically.
  2. For chart membership and Certified Fresh, configure the existing server MDBList API Key. Without a key these three ribbons are off; Oscar/Emmy use Wikidata without a key.
  3. Run Refresh Awards Tags in Dashboard → Scheduled Tasks → Jellyfin Enhanced. Its default daily trigger is 04:00, and the first refresh starts on its own when you turn Awards on. The task also works with Server-Side Tag Cache off. Under Groups → Awards, What it needs shows whether the MDBList key is set and when the task last ran.
  4. Each existing user enables Awards in Media Tags → Groups. New users take the admin default. Set its position, priority and Show up to limit like other groups (two by default, or All).
Administrator setting Default Behavior Enable Awards Tags Off Gates enrichment and the group's admin starting default; existing users retain their switch IMDb Top 250 / Certified Fresh / Oscar Winner / Emmy Winner / Letterboxd Top 250 On while enabled Selects which facts to fetch and which ribbons may appear IMDb Top 250 MDBList id or owner/slug aramil89/imdb-top-250 An MDBList list (not an IMDb link), numeric list IDs are accepted too Letterboxd Top 250 MDBList id or owner/slug abdulwahabaa/letterboxd-top-250 Configurable community list; only ranks 1–250 qualify Refresh interval (hours) 24 Fact/list freshness, clamped to 1–168 hours; adjust the scheduled task trigger too for a shorter cadence

The default IMDb and Letterboxd lists are maintained by MDBList users. Their availability, order and accuracy can change; a displayed rank is the configured list's rank. Replace the id/slug with a preferred maintained list as needed. An invalid or unavailable list fails independently; it does not become an empty successful chart.

Refreshes happen on the server, never per card. Chart requests and batched certification requests respect MDBList's existing account reserve. Wikidata queries share the detail-page awards cache (180-day positive, 30-day confirmed-negative, one-hour failure retry), with one actual query at a time, at least one second apart and provider Retry-After backoff. Refresh cancellation stops pending requests. Provider failures retain the last good facts for the same configuration and retry after an hour. Changing the key, lists or ribbon switches retires incompatible facts until refreshed. Facts and lists survive server restarts in award-tags.json; no key is written there.

Awards belongs to the exact movie or series, so seasons and episodes do not inherit a series win. Wikidata coverage is incomplete; no known win produces no winner chip. Unknown ceremony years omit the year. Spoiler Guard removes Awards wherever it strips score facts. Batch fallback and Native Poster Tags consume the same cached facts; native posters draw Awards in Corners and Bands with the same caps and order as the web. Static images cannot show hover details. All five labels and the whole Awards group have colours in Tag Styles.

The bundled simplified source marks and award silhouettes provide the same paths on web and native posters without remote logo downloads. They are nominative identification, distributed under this project's GPL-3.0 terms; award/service trademarks remain with their owners. See the asset generator and its provenance table. The existing detail-page CDN award logos remain independent.

docs.title: Logo Tags
docs.text:
Logo Tags show where a title streams, or the TV network or studio behind it, as one small logo on the card. Provider logos sit on a dark pill, network and studio logos on a light one so dark logos stay readable over any poster. A title without a logo image shows its name instead, shortened to its initials when it is long (Home Box Office → HBO).

How to use:

  1. Turn on the Logos group on the Groups tab of Media Tags. Choose its position and Show up to like any other group.
  2. Administrators choose what the logo shows under Media Tags settings → Groups → Logos.
Setting Default What it does Admin: Enable Logo Tags / personal: Logos switch Off Shows the Logos group; the admin value is the starting value for new users Admin / personal: Position Bottom left The group's corner or anchor in the Corners layout. Bands puts it in the top band, Caption in the caption strip, Summary and Minimal in the hover reveal Admin: Movies show Streaming service (studio when none) Streaming service, Studio or No logo Admin: Series show Network Network, Streaming service (network when none) or No logo. Seasons and episodes show their series' logo Admin: Streaming region Empty (the Seerr default region, else US) Two-letter country code whose subscription services count Admin: Logos per title 1 1 or 2; personal Show up to can show fewer Where the logos come from
  • Streaming service: the title's subscription (flat-rate) services in the region, from TMDB's watch providers, in TMDB's order. Titles that no service streams there show their studio or network instead.
  • Network and studio: the names Jellyfin has for the item (its studios), with the matching TMDB network or production-company logo when TMDB has one; otherwise the name.
  • The server looks titles up with the TMDB API Key from the Elsewhere settings and keeps each answer for a day. Full tag cache builds and the daily Refresh Tag Cache fetch new and expired lookups in small, rate-limited batches; a failed lookup is retried after an hour. A newly added item gets its logo when its cache entry is built, and the batch lookup used with the server cache off waits at most three seconds for it.
  • Logo images are downloaded by the server once and served from its own cache (/JellyfinEnhanced/logo/…), so browsers never contact TMDB. Without a TMDB key or internet access the server cannot look anything up: cards show the studio or network names Jellyfin has, as name chips.
  • Turning the group on for the first user, or changing the administrator's choices, refreshes the logos of every cached item in the background. With the server tag cache on, the page you turned the group on from shows the logos once that refresh lands (it checks for a few minutes), without a reload.

Native Poster Tags draw the same logos from the server's image cache, and the name chip when an image is not cached yet; a poster request never waits for TMDB, it queues the lookup or image in the background and the poster is redrawn once it arrives. Spoiler Guard's Hide tags removes the logos from protected items like their genres, on web cards, batch lookups and native posters. All browser fallback groups share the server-issued StripRevision, validated centrally for both memory and saved copies. Only unguarded (none) answers survive page loads; guarded answers stay on the current page, and unknown authority causes a fresh lookup. Logos the browser remembers (with the server tag cache off, or its local fallback on) carry that revision: after you protect or unprotect an item, or switch Hide tags, they are fetched again instead of being redrawn. Tag Styles colour the pills on the Logos tab. Custom CSS can target .logo-overlay-container, .je-logo-chip and its data-je-logo-kind / data-je-logo-style attributes (see CSS Customization).

docs.title: Custom Tags
docs.text:
Custom Tags turn your own Jellyfin metadata into poster chips. The administrator writes rules: items that carry a Jellyfin tag (for example 4K Remaster) or belong to a collection (for example Criterion) get a chip with the rule's label and, optionally, an icon. Tags are the ones in each item's metadata (Edit metadata → Tags, or imported keywords).

How to use — administrators:

  1. Open Media Tags settings → Groups → Custom.
  2. Click Add rule. Choose Tag or Collection, then type the name: suggestions list the library's tags or collections. Enter the chip's Label and pick an Icon if you want one.
  3. Complete rows save automatically. Colour each label under Colours → Custom.
  4. Enable Custom Tags and its Position set the starting values for users, like the other groups.

How to use — personal preferences: turn on the Custom group on the Groups tab of Media Tags and choose its position and limit, like any other group.

Setting Default What it does Admin: Enable Custom Tags / personal: Custom switch Off Shows a chip for each rule an item matches Admin: Custom tag rules None Up to 20 rules: Match (Tag or Collection), the tag or collection name, a Label of up to 24 characters and an optional Icon from the genre icon set Show up to 3 Chips beyond the limit are left out, as for other groups

Names match exactly but ignore case and extra spaces. Chips follow the rule order in the table, and reordering the rules takes effect at once; a rule whose name matches nothing simply shows no chip. Seasons and episodes take their series' tags and collections as well as their own. A collection chip only shows for users who can open that collection: if library access or parental controls hide the collection from someone, its chip is hidden on its items too, even on items they can see. Hovering a chip shows its label; administrators also see the tag or collection it came from. Other users never receive the tag or collection names a rule uses. Spoiler Guard treats custom chips like genres: when it hides tags (Hide tags, unless the user's own override keeps them), guarded items show no custom chips, since a tag or collection can give away the plot. With the server tag cache off, the browser keeps custom matches between page loads only for users with nothing guarded. A guard set on another device therefore takes effect on the next page load. Rule edits reach native posters at once, the server tag cache on or off: a poster drawn after the save matches its item against the new rules (label and icon edits keep the matches as they are). The server checks the rules when you save: it drops incomplete rows, unknown match types and labels made only of punctuation in any script (such as *, which the table flags), trims names and labels, shortens long labels and merges rows that name the same tag or collection.

When chips update

The server tag cache records which rules each item matches. Editing an item's tags, adding items to or removing them from a collection, renaming or deleting a collection, or changing a series' tags updates its chips (and its seasons' and episodes') within seconds. Saving rules that match something new re-checks the whole cache in the background, without reading media files; changing only a label, icon or colour takes effect at once. The nightly reconcile and a full rebuild catch anything else.

With the server tag cache off, chips come from each card's batched tag data and match tags only: collection membership needs the cache. Browsers remember an item's chips only while the rules stay the same.

docs.title: People Tags
docs.text:
People Tags add age and birthplace facts to cast and guest-cast cards on item detail pages. They support rectangular and round portraits.

How to use:

  1. Turn on Show People Tags in Media Tags → Layout.
  2. Open a title's detail page and view its cast.

Administrators can set the starting value in Media Tags.

Setting Default What it does Admin: Enable People Tags / personal: Show People Tags Off Adds age chips, birthplace information, and deceased styling to cast cards Admin: Tags Cache Duration (days) 30 Sets the lifetime of cached person facts in the browser; allowed range 1–365

You'll see green current-age chips, red age-at-death chips, and blue age-at-release chips near the top of a rectangular portrait. Birthplace appears along the bottom, with a country flag when the place can be resolved. Deceased people receive a cross and grayscale styling; round portraits use an adjusted layout.

Optional TMDB enrichment

To add facts from TMDB, the person needs a TMDB ID and your administrator must set TMDB API Key under Elsewhere & Reviews.

Person metadata and caching

Facts come from Jellyfin person metadata. Failed or unavailable TMDB enrichment keeps usable Jellyfin facts. Missing birth/death dates or birthplace omit the corresponding details. Age at release also needs the viewed item's visible premiere date; hidden or stripped dates cannot supply it.

Age at release is calculated from birth to premiere without a death-date limit. For a posthumous release, that chip can show an age the person never reached.

Birthplace flags require the last comma-separated part of the place to match a recognized country name. A place ending in England UK can therefore show its text without a flag.

The separate browser facts cache holds at most 3,000 people. Ages are calculated from cached dates for the current visit rather than kept as stale age numbers. People Tags are web cast overlays and are not drawn by Native Poster Tags. Spoiler Guard can remove protected guest-cast/cast cards before these overlays appear.

docs.title: Player badges
docs.text:
You can show scores in the web video player's controls and an age-classification badge when playback starts. These are independent server settings; neither has a personal control in the panel.

How to use:

  1. Configure score chips on the Media Tags admin tab (Groups → Rating, which also holds Show the rating in the video player).
  2. Configure the playback-start classification badge under Playback → Player Behaviour.
  3. Save the playback setting on the main page; Media Tags edits save automatically. Refresh the web client.
Setting Default What it does Show Rating in Video Player On Shows community and critic score chips near the time information in the on-screen controls, before Ends at Show Age Rating When Playback Starts Off When an official classification is available, shows it with up to three recognized advisory tags and up to three genres when playback starts

Neither setting requires poster Rating Tags or Age Rating Tags. Poster scope switches do not control player score chips.

Player score and classification behavior

Player score chips use Jellyfin's rating fields and can fall back to series scores when a season/episode has neither score.

The playback-start badge needs an official classification. It uses the series' classification when an episode has none. It displays for five seconds, followed by a 400 ms fade.

Advisories are selected from matching Jellyfin metadata tags. Episodes also use series genres when their own are missing and incorporate series tags. Missing advisories or genres omit only their respective lines. Colored Ratings Backgrounds can color its classification box.

docs.title: Languages
docs.text:
Media Tags follow the language Jellyfin Enhanced's text uses (your Jellyfin display language, else the Jellyfin Enhanced display language, else the browser's):

What Web Native posters Chip words (status badges, Dual/Multi, Mixed, editions such as Extended, award captions such as Oscar Winner) Your language The language saved with your web settings (the one their dates use) Scores (8,1 in German, Persian digits in Persian) Your language's decimal separator and digits Same, from the saved language; text is laid out with the Unicode bidirectional algorithm, as the browser draws it: numbers read left to right in Arabic and Persian, Hebrew or Arabic words mixed with numbers or Latin names keep their reading order, and bracket pairs resolve together Dates (Airs Nov 6) and time zones Your language and the browser's time zone The saved language and time zone Language names in tooltips (Audio: japonais) Your language No tooltips Codecs, sources, resolutions, brand names (HEVC, REMUX, 4K, IMDb Top 250) Unchanged Unchanged

A string not yet translated into your language appears in English. Translations come from the project's Weblate contributors; most Media Tags strings are new and only in English so far. To see how far each language is, run node scripts/tag-translation-coverage.mjs in a checkout: it lists the translated Media Tags strings per language, and the test suite checks that every translated string keeps the {placeholders} of the English one.

docs.title: Server-Side Tag Cache
docs.text:
The server cache prepares tags for supported items in included libraries, so each page avoids repeating metadata requests. You receive only data allowed by your library access and Spoiler Guard policy. Each entry also records the item's library (a season's or episode's is its series'), which tag look rules match on.

How to use:

  1. Leave Server-side tag cache on (Media Tags admin tab → Server). Choose library exclusions if needed.
  2. After changing exclusions, or after a plugin update that changes tag computation, click Rebuild cache there (or on the Overview tab).
  3. Confirm the full rebuild. The Overview shows Rebuilding until it is done, keeps showing it if you reload the page meanwhile, and says so when the rebuild finishes.
  4. Check server logs for progress and completion. The existing cache keeps serving while the new one builds in the background.

Browser fallback controls appear only with the server tag cache off.

Setting Default What it does Server-Side Tag Cache On Loads, builds, and maintains the server cache; off uses per-page batch fallback Exclude libraries from the tag cache Off Reveals library selection for omitting libraries from precomputation Libraries to exclude Empty Selects libraries to skip on the next full rebuild; an empty selection excludes nothing Tags Cache Duration (days) 30 Lifetime of browser fallback entries and People Tags facts, not the server cache's refresh schedule; range 1–365 Persist Tag Fallback Cache in Browser Storage Off in configuration Visible only with Server-Side Tag Cache off; saving in that mode forces it on. See Browser storage and fallback below Clear All Client Caches Action Visible here only with Server-Side Tag Cache off; signals clients to invalidate JE caches on their next load. Does not rebuild the server snapshot or reset server-stored personal preferences

docs.title: Builds, refreshes, and exclusions
docs.text:
The retained cache grows with the number of included items. Exclude large libraries or disable server mode if its memory cost is unsuitable.

Jellyfin compresses the cache response with Brotli or gzip, so a browser downloads about a tenth of its JSON size. On a 3,882-entry test library a full download was 14.7 MB of JSON and 1.39 MB on the wire, about 3.8 KB and 360 bytes per entry; entries have since grown to about 4.6 KB (3,892 entries, November 2026). At that size 50,000 entries are roughly 230 MB of JSON and, compressed as before, about 22 MB to download. The browser reads a full download in pages of 2,000 entries, so no response or parse holds the whole library. Up to 20,000 entries it keeps them in memory and stores a copy afterwards. Past that it writes what it holds, and then each page as it arrives, straight into its stored copy and keeps none of them, so a load never holds more than 20,000 entries plus one page; once the copy is complete it reads entries from it as cards need them. A load that keeps seeing the cache change underneath starts over twice, after short pauses, then leaves the cards to batch lookups until the next navigation tries again; it never asks for the whole cache in one response. After a load it fetches only changed entries, and removed items arrive as a list of ids.

scripts/bench-tag-cache.mjs measures this on a synthetic library whose entries carry the real ones' fields (about 4.2 KB of JSON each; the run prints the size). Memory is the heap still held after each page once garbage is collected, in Node; a browser's own peak (with IndexedDB's copies in flight) is somewhat higher. On a desktop with Node 26:

Synthetic library One response Pages of 2,000 Memory kept 50,000 entries, 203.3 MB of JSON one 203.3 MB body, one 1.7 s parse largest body 8.3 MB, longest parse 48 ms at most 102.5 MB kept between pages while loading (pages streamed into the stored copy past 20,000); 254.0 MB when every page was held until the copy was written 100,000 entries, 407.2 MB of JSON one 407.2 MB body, one 3.0 s parse largest body 8.3 MB, longest parse 57 ms at most 102.5 MB kept between pages; 508.7 MB when every page was held

On the server, every page of a full load reads one shared, sorted list of the cache's keys, made once and made again only when an item is added or removed, instead of sorting the rest of the library for each page. An opt-in benchmark in the backend tests (PrivacyCachePagingBenchmark, run with JE_BENCH_TAG_CACHE=1) pages through 200,000 entries in about 0.3 s for an account that sees everything (100 pages, four such loads at once in about the same time), where sorting the rest of the library for every page took about 4 s for the keys alone.

Without a stored copy (private browsing, storage blocked or full), a library of up to 20,000 entries stays in memory and the next page load downloads it again; a larger one is not held at all: cards ask for their tags in batches of up to 200 for the rest of the session. Each browser profile downloads in full once, then again only after a full rebuild, more than 20,000 removals between rebuilds, a Spoiler Guard change, or an access change that makes an item visible the browser has not stored (a library or parental limit opened up). When the user can only see less (an item added where they cannot see it, library access removed, an item re-rated above their limit), the next update carries the list of ids they can still see, and the browser drops the rest and clears their tags from the cards on screen. Any update redraws the cards on screen whose items it changed; the other cards keep their tags. If you put Jellyfin behind a reverse proxy, let it pass Accept-Encoding through so compression stays on.

Cache lifecycle and excluded libraries

When poster review chips are enabled, visible review averages travel with the filtered cache data.

At startup, JE restores tag-cache.json from <PluginsPath>/configurations/Jellyfin.Plugin.JellyfinEnhanced/. If no usable cache is available, it queues Refresh Tag Cache to build one. Library item additions, updates, and removals keep entries current. A series edit that changes its scores, age rating or genres also updates the seasons and episodes that take them from it (re-reading their metadata, not their media), on the same update or reconcile; native posters built while the cache is off drop those children's remembered entries at once. The scheduled task normally reconciles changes rather than recomputing every item. Its default daily trigger is 03:00.

Excluded libraries do not lose access or forcibly lose their web tags. Cards without a server entry can use per-page batch fallback. Exclusions also bypass the normal cache-update audio-language synchronization path; the standalone language-sync task can still process those items.

Builds load item data in small pages to reduce peak memory.

Audio languages that JE reads from Matroska track headers (for regional tags such as pt-BR) are kept in matroska-languages.json next to the tag cache, keyed by file path, size and modification time. Later rebuilds, reconciles and tag-data requests do not open an unchanged file again, which matters on network and cloud mounts where each open can download a large read-ahead.

Turning server mode off releases the in-memory cache and stops loading, building, monitoring, and scheduled refresh work. The saved snapshot remains on disk. Clients pick up the switch on their next load.

Re-enabling from the dashboard restores the snapshot and catches up on missed changes in the background, without a restart.

If you edit the configuration file by hand instead, restart Jellyfin and run Refresh Tag Cache to catch up.

docs.title: Browser storage and fallback
docs.text:
Turn off Server-side tag cache to reveal Keep a tag cache in each browser and Clear all browser caches in the Server section of the Media Tags admin tab (the configuration page's Overview keeps a quick action for the clear signal).

Browser storage and fallback details

The first web load downloads the server payload and saves an IndexedDB copy scoped to that server and user. Later loads restore that copy and request changes since the saved cursor. Tags wait for confirmation that the stored version and access/Spoiler Guard revision still match. A rebuild or changed filtering replaces the copy, including changes made from another device. Navigation also checks for updates, with requests spaced during rapid browsing.

A copy written before the entry format last changed (version 11 added the library) is not restored; the browser downloads the cache again.

The stored copy is invalidated when server mode is switched off, by Clear All Client Caches, or when another account signs in in the same browser. Each copy contains that user's filtered, spoiler-safe data.

Without usable IndexedDB, including some private modes or storage failures, the client downloads the payload again on each page load and uses memory only.

Saving with the server cache off forces Persist Tag Fallback Cache in Browser Storage on. The client enables localStorage fallback whenever server mode is off.

Batch fallback fetches the items needed for the current page and keeps frequently used entries in memory. Every group validates its fallback data against the server-issued StripRevision through the shared renderer base. Only authoritative none entries persist in localStorage using Tags Cache Duration (days); guarded entries are page-only, and unknown or mismatched revisions require fresh data. This is separate from the full server-payload copy in IndexedDB. Browser storage failures leave tags able to fetch data again. Average-review lookups in fallback mode are batched separately.

For rules and locked items, the batch lookup's type, series, library, genres and age rating of each item are remembered beside those entries (JE_tagLookFacts, at most 3,000 items, newest kept). Like the per-tag entries, they belong to the signed-in user and are dropped when another account signs in or by Clear All Client Caches.

docs.title: Card identity and shared artwork
docs.text: Web badges describe the card's item, even when an episode displays a season or series poster. Loading the artwork later does not change which item's tags appear. Cards without a valid item identifier can still use the poster URL as a fallback.

docs.title: Tags after navigation
docs.text: With the server cache off, cards still waiting for a batch fetch are retried after navigation. Season cards added as a series page opens receive tags without a reload; completed cards keep their tags.

docs.title: Related routes
docs.text:
Diagnostic routes

These routes are useful when diagnosing a cache problem; routine setup uses the dashboard controls above. All require authentication. See the API reference for broader API use.

Route Access and behavior GET /JellyfinEnhanced/tag-cache/{userId} Own account or administrator; filtered cache payload. Returns 404 when server mode is off. Optional since is a Unix-millisecond cursor; use the returned generation timestamp, not servedAt POST /JellyfinEnhanced/tag-data/{userId} Own account or administrator; per-page fallback for accessible items. Body is a nonempty array of at most 200 item-ID strings; optional mediaSourceId selects a media version; optional latestEpisode=true adds the newest episode's added date to series and seasons GET /JellyfinEnhanced/status-tags/series?ids=… Signed-in caller; up to 50 accessible series IDs, returning TMDB status and last/next aired facts GET /JellyfinEnhanced/status-tags/trending Any signed-in user; the shared trending list for Status Tags. Empty while the admin has Status Tags or the trending rank off POST /JellyfinEnhanced/tag-cache/rebuild Administrator only; starts a full background rebuild. Returns 400 with server mode off, or 409 if a rebuild is already running GET /JellyfinEnhanced/audio-language-tags?codes=… Returns base/regional synchronized tag names for the supplied comma-separated language codes; empty mapping when sync is off

docs.title: Native Poster Tags (Experimental)
docs.text:
Native Poster Tags add your enabled poster groups to images shown in eligible native apps, without changing the original artwork files. The feature is built into JE, so you need no companion plugin or client modification.

Server preview; this is not a native-app screenshot.

Personalized native image responses for the same movie: Corners (left), Bands (right). These are composited posters, not physical-device screenshots.

Web (left) and the real Jellyfin Android TV 0.19.10 app in the emulator (right): Flush Corners with Compact labels (top) and Status at left centre with Quality at right centre (bottom). The app dims unfocused cards.

How to use:

  1. Enable suitable tag groups and ensure the items have the required metadata.
  2. On the Media Tags admin tab → Server, turn on Native poster tags (experimental).
  3. Each user can opt out with Show Tags in Native Clients (Experimental) in Media Tags → Layout.
  4. Reopen the native app's library or restart the app to pick up changed poster addresses.

Setting Default What it does Admin: Native poster tags (experimental) Off Server-wide master switch; off serves original posters and stops native tag composition Admin: Additional excluded apps Empty Adds web-wrapper client names that should retain original posters; newline- or comma-separated Personal: Show Tags in Native Clients (Experimental) On while allowed Shows tags in native clients; hidden while the master switch is off, retaining the saved choice Stored native preferences

The admin configuration uses NativePosterTagsEnabled and NativePosterTagsWebClientNames for the master switch and additional client exclusions. The personal UseNativePosterTags value permits native tags when null or true; false opts out while retaining the preference when the master switch is off.

Enable the tag groups too

The master switch alone does not produce visible tags: each user's applicable groups start off.

Supported groups and preferences

JE draws tags into Primary images for movies, series, seasons, episodes, collections, and videos. Supported groups are quality, genre, language, ratings, user-review, age-classification, Awards, Status, Logos and Custom. People Tags are not a native group.

It uses personal tag switches, audio/subtitle includes, Flags/Codes style and Dual/Multi badge mode, quality categories/order, sound-language preference, each group's Where to show item-type switches, score includes, together with the personal language-priority policy (or the live administrator fallback). Native posters draw Corners or Bands from your saved default layout. Both respect the chosen Full or Compact label density, as on the web; version-0 (legacy) accounts keep their previous labels. Corners supports all nine anchors, hidden groups, your explicit group order (otherwise the original stacking order) and limits. Bands uses its own top/bottom/hidden profile, priority order and limits. Its translucent gradient strips keep the middle clear; the first top group starts left and later groups align right. Each strip fits at most two rows. The bottom strip shows chips in priority order until the first one with no room, as on the web, and counts the rest in +N; only a chip that could never fit is skipped on its own. The overflow chip uses the web’s 11px bold style multiplied by tag size and reserves the total-count width before bottom-band selection, then displays the actual omitted count. Caption, Summary and Minimal fall back to the saved Corners profile with Full labels because native images have no title block or hover surface. Per-item locks, server-wide item looks and tag look rules apply natively (each look gets its own poster variant); shape overrides remain web features, because an image request does not say what shape of card shows it.

Centre-anchor differences: in the centre slots (top and bottom centre, left and right centre, and centre), native posters omit whole chips that do not fit and show a fitting +N count for them; the count is left out when its own box cannot fit. A static image has no hover or focus, so the count cannot reveal the hidden names as the web's tooltip does. The first chip in a centre anchor stays visible with an ellipsis when necessary, keeping its original typography; subsequent chips that do not fit are omitted. The image request cannot reproduce the web card's progress bar, Jellyfin indicators or custom overlays; native placement uses the saved default Bands or Corners profile, the item's own look or the matching rule's. The four default corner positions are unchanged.

docs.title: Eligible clients and requests
docs.text:
Examples of native clients include Jellyfin for Android TV, Tizen, Swiftfin, Findroid, and Streamyfin.

The built-in exclusions are Jellyfin Web, Jellyfin Media Player, Jellium Desktop, Jellyfin Desktop, Jellyfin for WebOS, Jellyfin for Android (the phone app), Jellyfin iOS and Jellyfin iPadOS. These load web overlays and retain original poster images. Jellyfin for Android TV is a different client name and is eligible.

If a custom web wrapper shows tags twice, add its name as shown under Dashboard → Devices to Additional excluded apps.

Client matching and image requests

Native tags depend on the app retaining Jellyfin's personalized image tag in its poster request. Requests that omit it, or ask Jellyfin to draw its own watched/progress/unplayed-count indicators into the image, retain original artwork.

Exclusion matching trims whitespace and compares exact names without case sensitivity. Unidentified clients are excluded.

docs.title: Limits and caching
docs.text:
Layout, Spoiler Guard, and image caching
  • Static layout: genre hover names and Hide tags on hover do not apply. Size follows the image width rather than the app's final display size; landscape episode images use an adjusted layout.
  • No page or row context: Disable Tags on Search Page and the Continue Watching row / Next Up row switches of Where to show do not apply. Its item-type switches still apply. Tags can appear anywhere the app reuses that Primary image, including search and detail pages. If an episode card uses a series poster, its tags describe that image's owner.
  • Spoiler-safe data: native composition applies the user's Spoiler Guard stripping policy. Artwork follows the configured stock-card/blur policy, rather than always using blur. Spoiler-scoped responses use no-store so an old poster is not retained under a changed policy.
  • Remote status: cold or expired trending/schedule snapshots omit remote badges for that render and refresh in the background; image delivery never waits for TMDB. Queued series schedules refresh in batches of 16, up to four TMDB lookups at once within the shared rate limit, and each batch shows on the next poster request as soon as it finishes.
  • First-view cost: the server draws a poster the first time a particular variant/size is requested. Rendered images are cached with a 128 MiB memory budget and approximately 1 GiB disk budget under Jellyfin's cache directory, jellyfin-enhanced/poster-tags.
  • Status dates and language: saving personal preferences in the web client with Status enabled remembers that user's date locale and timezone. Native labels use that saved context; until then they use the JE display language (English fallback) and the server timezone. TMDB dates remain plain calendar dates, as on the web. Another native device cannot supply its own browser timezone through an image request. Short month/day dates use browser-generated locale patterns, month names, calendars and digits for the shipped languages and their regional variants (including en-IN, es-419 and fr-CA). An unlisted variant uses its closest culture ancestor. Saved Unicode locale extensions are retained, while native formatting uses their base language/script/region. Status text uses Tag Styles' Status group and individual badge colours; static chips do not apply the web backdrop blur.
  • Status freshness: posters with a visible Status group use five-minute URL buckets and an HTTP cache lifetime capped to the remaining URL bucket (whole seconds; sub-second remaining lifetime is served uncached), even with the server tag cache off. Date-window and local-midnight changes appear within five minutes after a fresh metadata/image request. A URL keeps drawing its tags through the next bucket too (status as of the request), so a poster requested just after a bucket boundary is not untagged; a client retaining a URL longer than that must refresh library metadata, and older tokens serve original artwork until then. The server draws a poster again only when the badge it shows changes: its stored composite is keyed by the resolved Status badge (and the filtered parent facts), not by the URL bucket, so a new URL for an unchanged poster is served from the stored image. Text and family colours enter the tile key. No live status data is persisted in the tag cache and its schema is unchanged.
  • Refreshes: settings changes can change poster addresses. With the server tag cache on, tag-data changes also change addresses for cached items. Apps can need a library refresh or restart to use them. With the cache off, tag-data changes keep the same URL; apps can show the old composite for up to an hour before revalidating that URL.
  • Fallback: unsupported identity/token requests, missing renderable tags, decode/render failures, sources over 32 MiB, or decoded image sides outside 32–4096 pixels can yield original artwork. These are implementation limits, not adjustable settings.
Signing key and backups

JE stores a 32-byte signing secret in <PluginsPath>/configurations/Jellyfin.Plugin.JellyfinEnhanced/native-poster-tags.key, separately from rendered-image caches. Preserve it in backups to retain personalized URL-signing continuity. JE recreates a missing or invalid key. Older URLs can then serve original artwork until clients refresh.

If the key cannot be persisted, JE logs a warning and uses a process-lifetime key that changes after restart.

On Unix, new keys use owner-only read/write permissions. There is no setting for this internal key.

Administrator preview route

Administrators can diagnose composition with GET /JellyfinEnhanced/native-poster-tags/preview/{itemId}. It requires an accessible supported item, an existing target user, and a local Primary image.

Optional userId defaults to the caller. width defaults to 360, and width/optional height are clamped to 32–2048. Optional topRightOffset controls indicator clearance.

The JPEG response uses no-store and includes X-JE-Poster-Tags-* diagnostics.

The preview attempts composition even with the master/personal native switch off. It strips tag data for Spoiler Guard but uses original, unblurred artwork. It therefore does not preview image protection.

Server-wide item look edits preserve unrelated changes made by another administrator while saving. Removing a look and immediately choosing Undo cancels that edit. After an uncertain save failure, Undo stays pending until the server acknowledges the restored look. Server import and its Undo replace the complete item-look list, including when both lists contain 500 different entries. Edits made while a replacement is still saving or awaiting Retry become part of that replacement; Keep mine and Take theirs resolve the complete list.

docs.title: Tag Styles and CSS
docs.text:
Use Tag Styles to recolour poster tags without writing CSS. You pick a preset, then adjust a whole group of tags or a single tag. The same colours reach the web overlays and the posters drawn for native apps.

How to use:

  1. Open the Colours section of the Media Tags admin tab and turn on Use these tag colours.
  2. Under Apply to, choose Web, Native posters or Both.
  3. Pick a Preset. It applies straight away and keeps any group or tag colours you set. The presets are always shown. Under the group tabs, Preset for this group gives one group its own preset (for example the Poster preset on Status only); Same as the design follows the main one.
  4. Choose a group tab (Quality, Age, Rating, Genre, Status, Language, Awards, Logos, Custom), then Whole group or one tag.
  5. Set Background, Border and Text with a swatch or any colour, and an Opacity of 40–100% on its own row. Watch the contrast badge and the preview; every status badge can be coloured, not only the first few.
  6. Each edit saves on its own. Refresh web clients to see the change; native posters redraw the next time they load.

Setting Default What it does Use these tag colours Off Turns the colours on. Turning it off keeps your edits Apply to Both Web recolours the overlays in Jellyfin Web; Native posters recolours the tags drawn into posters for apps such as Android TV (needs Native poster tags (experimental)) Preset Default The colours every tag starts from (see below) Let users pick their own preset Off Adds the Colours tab to each user's Media Tags section. Your group and tag colours stay on top of the preset a user picks Reset all colours Clears every group and tag colour and returns to the Default preset after a confirmation; Undo in the message brings them back

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
Each preset sets a background, border and text colour for every kind of tag. Each preset tile previews a 4K, a rating and a PG-13 tag in its colours.

Preset Look Default The built-in colours. Nothing changes and custom CSS keeps working as before Glass Light translucent chips with a soft white border; white text, gold community scores and trending ranks, red critic scores Outline Dark translucent chips; the border and text take each tag's tint: blue resolution, orange dynamic range and IMAX/3D, green audio, grey codec and source, gold community score, red critic score, the board colour for age ratings. Genre, status and language get a white border Dark Near-black chips without a border; white text with gold and red scores Light Near-white chips without a border; dark text, darker gold and red scores, age ratings in their board colour Mono Neutral dark grey chips with light grey text and a faint border Poster Each tag takes its colour from the poster it sits on: the artwork's main colour, kept saturated (a red poster gives red tags) and darkened or lightened just enough that white or black text reads at 4.5:1 or better; a grey or very dark poster gives a neutral dark tag. The border is a lighter or darker shade of the same colour. Flags keep their own look

docs.title: The Poster preset
docs.text:
The colour comes from the artwork your browser is already showing (never the blurred placeholder shown while it loads): a 32px copy is read once, in idle time, and the result is remembered per poster in the browser, so scrolling back is instant. A new poster image for an item is read again. Nothing is sent anywhere. If the browser cannot read an image (for example artwork served from another site), that poster keeps the Default colours. Native posters work out the same colour from the image they draw on.

Group and tag colours you set stay on top, field by field: set a group's text to white and every tag of the group keeps white text over its poster colour. Default on a row hands that field back to the poster. Because the colours depend on the artwork, the contrast check shows the worst case Poster can produce, and the preview shows the colours of a red poster.

docs.title: Groups and single tags
docs.text:
The editor shows every tag of the selected group in its current colours, so you can see the result before changing anything. A dot marks a group or tag you changed.

Tab Tags you can edit one by one Notes Quality Every quality label (4K, HDR10, ATMOS, TRUEHD ATMOS, DD+ ATMOS, HEVC…) Combined labels such as ATMOS 7.1 follow their base label; TRUEHD ATMOS and DD+ ATMOS are labels of their own that start with the ATMOS colours Age One chip per age rating colour board, shown with a sample rating Hover a chip to see every rating it covers Rating Community, Critic, User review Rating chips have no border of their own: a border colour draws a thin inner ring Genre Every genre with an icon of its own and Other (see Genre colours) Text colours the icon; a genre with colours of its own also colours its name beside it on hover Status Just Added, New Movie, New Series, New Episode, Trending, schedule, milestone and series-state badges Applies to web and native posters. A Trending text colour also recolours the rank Awards IMDb Top 250, Certified Fresh, Oscar Winner, Emmy Winner, Letterboxd Top 250 Bundled logos keep their source colours; the chip background, text and border can change Language Flag image, Language codes, Subtitles, Dual / Multi, Dual, Multi, and individual ISO language codes Chips share the quality-chip box and take background, border and text colours. Flag images keep only their border ring; partial flags keep their dashed outline Logos Provider logo, Network / studio logo, Name chip Colours the pill behind the logo; Text colours the name chip

| Custom | Each label of the Custom tag rules | The labels follow the rules table as you edit it; rules that share a label share its colours. The icon takes the text colour |

A tag's colours are worked out field by field: its own colour if you set one, else the group colour, else the preset. Default on a row removes that one colour from what you are editing, so it falls back to the group or the preset.

docs.title: Genre colours
docs.text:
Each genre the icons know is its own tag on the Genre tab, shown as its icon (with its name where there is room; hover a tile for the name). Find a genre narrows the list. With the keyboard the tiles are a single stop: the arrow keys move the selection, Home and End jump to the first and last tile. A genre and its other spellings and translations share one tag, so colouring Comedy also colours Comédie and Komödie. Genres without an icon of their own (for example Anime or Children) use Other. Genre names are matched without regard to case.

Poster preset with three coloured genres: Animation blue, Family green, Comedy yellow; every other tag takes its poster's colour.

The genre's colours apply to its icon on web cards and native posters alike; on the web, the name that appears beside the icon on hover, in the caption strip and in the Summary and Minimal hover lists, takes them too. Only a genre you colour on its own does that: Whole group colours and presets colour every icon but leave the names in their usual dark pill. The preview shows a Horror, a Comedy and an Animation icon. Documents saved before genres had their own tags (one colour for every genre) open with that colour as the Whole group colour, so nothing changes until you colour a genre.

docs.title: Contrast check
docs.text:
The badge under the colour rows rates the text against the background, both shown over a dark poster:

Badge Contrast Meaning AA (green) 4.5:1 or more Easy to read AA large only (amber) 3:1 to 4.5:1 Readable for large or bold text only Low contrast (red) under 3:1 Hard to read

With Whole group selected, the badge only appears when a tag reads under 3:1, and names the tag that reads worst. Pick a single tag to see its own rating. Translucent presets also depend on the artwork behind them, so check the preview. Under Poster, a tag whose text or background comes from the artwork is rated by the worst case over any artwork, and the badge says so; a tag whose text and background are both set here is rated by those colours, and Whole group shows whichever reads worst.

docs.title: User presets
docs.text:
With Let users pick their own preset on, users choose Tag Colours on the Colours tab of Media Tags (see The Media Tags section). Server default follows your preset; any other choice replaces only the preset, never your group or tag colours. The web applies it right away, and native posters for that user follow the next time they load.

Styles change colours, not size, shape, position or visibility. For web layout, sizing, hiding and more detailed styling, see CSS Customization.

Style requirements

Native colours need Native poster tags (experimental). Enable the tag feature and supply metadata first: CSS cannot create missing tags or restyle pixels already drawn into an image.

Stored style configuration

The saved fields are TagStylesEnabled, TagStyleTarget (both, web or native), TagStylePreset (default, glass, outline, dark, light, mono or poster), TagStylesAllowUserPreset, and TagStyleOverrides: an empty string, or a version 2 document {"v":2,"preset":…,"groups":{…},"labels":{…}} holding only the colours you set. Settings saved before this editor (version 1, with colours per quality label, age board, rating chip and genre) still load and look exactly as before: each tag you had changed keeps the colours it was drawn with, and the preset becomes Default, because the old presets were already baked into those colours. They are converted to version 2 on the next save. TagStyleApplyScope is no longer used. Each user's choice is TagStylePreset in their settings (null follows the admin). Saving checks the document, in either version: anything that is not a colour, an unknown group, tag or field, or a document over 40 KB keeps the current styles. See the API reference for the full format.

Web CSS behavior

Saved Tag Styles use stronger important colour rules than simple CSS recipes, but sufficiently specific important custom CSS can override them. Status chips carry data-je-status (added, newMovie, newSeries, newEpisode, trending, or a schedule/milestone/series-state key such as season_finale) if you want to target one kind yourself. Prefer the corner controls to transforms that can disrupt shared-corner stacking. Genre-name styling requires Hide tags on hover off. Hiding a displayed flag with CSS does not make a fourth flag appear.

Style API routes

The effective web colours are available through authenticated GET /JellyfinEnhanced/tag-styles (empty when disabled or targeting native posters only; optional preset for a user's own preset). The shipped defaults and preset palettes come from authenticated GET /JellyfinEnhanced/tag-styles/catalog (any signed-in user; it holds only the shipped palettes, no settings).

docs.title: Related badge systems
docs.text: Other integrations have separate badge systems: see Seerr for request/availability/provider badges and *arr for service status and synchronized tag links. Those are configured independently of these poster groups.

docs.title: Contributing Translations
docs.text: Help translate JE's interface into your language or improve existing strings. You can contribute through Weblate without a local development setup.

docs.title: Translate on Weblate (Recommended)
docs.text:
Weblate keeps translation work in one place and provides quality checks.

  1. Open the Jellyfin Enhanced project on Weblate.
  2. Choose your language, or request a new language through the project.
  3. Translate or improve strings using the English source and available context.
  4. Review the validation feedback and save your changes.

Use the project engagement page to find languages that need help.

docs.title: Preserve functional text
docs.text:
Translate the visible wording while keeping the parts the interface needs to work. Use consistent wording across related controls. Check long strings in context where possible, especially buttons, notifications, and dialogs.

Note

Translate values, not JSON keys. Do not replace a missing translation with an empty string.

Details

Preserve these parts exactly:

  • Variables such as {count}, {query}, or {userName}. They may move within a sentence, but must retain their names and braces.
  • Icon tokens such as {{icon:search}}.
  • Functional HTML, such as <kbd>, <br>, and links. Translate visible text without breaking the markup or changing required attributes.
  • Escape sequences and valid JSON syntax. For example, a newline inside a JSON string is written as \n.

docs.title: Plural forms
docs.text:
A string that holds a count ({count}, {days}, {n}, {items}, {hours}, {minutes} or {seconds}) can have one form per CLDR plural category of your language: add the key with _zero, _one, _two, _few, _many or _other appended, next to the plain key. For example, English has "panel_media_tags_badge_window_added": "within {days} days of being added" and "panel_media_tags_badge_window_added_one": "within {days} day of being added".

The browser and the server-drawn posters both choose the form by your language's rules (Russian 21 is _one, 3 is _few, 5 is _many). A category your file has no form for uses _other, then the plain key, so the plain key should read correctly for the most common count. Forms keep the same variables as the plain key. English forms are never used for a sentence your file translates.

Weblate lists the keys the English file has, so it offers the _one forms. A category English does not need (_few, _many, _two, _zero) can be added to your language's file through the manual JSON route below; until then the plain key covers it.

docs.title: Maintainer Fallback: Manual JSON Changes
docs.text:
When Weblate is unavailable, maintainers can update locale JSON in the repository. Prefer the Weblate workflow for normal contributions so edits stay coordinated.

  1. Work in Jellyfin.Plugin.JellyfinEnhanced/js/locales/.
  2. For an existing language, edit its JSON file. For a new language, copy en.json and name the file with its language code, such as es.json; follow the existing naming convention for regional variants.
  3. Translate string values while preserving keys, placeholders, icon tokens, and functional markup.

  4. From the repository root, validate the changed language:

    node scripts/validate-translations.js validate es

    Replace es with your language code. To validate every locale:

    node scripts/validate-translations.js validate

  5. Fix errors and review warnings, then submit a pull request describing the language and changes.

A passing check does not replace reviewing grammar, meaning, or layout.

How it works

The validator compares locales with en.json. Missing keys are errors; extra keys and empty strings produce warnings. For source strings that contain placeholders, missing placeholders are errors and extra placeholders produce warnings.

It does not detect added placeholders in a string whose English source has none, so review those manually. Validation errors return a nonzero exit status.

docs.title: Translation Updates
docs.text:
Merged translations normally reach your installed plugin with a plugin release. They do not immediately replace translations included with the version you already have.

  1. To select a language, open personal Settings → Language Settings → Display Language.
  2. Choose your language. JE saves your choice to your account and browser, then reloads the page.

Clear Translation Cache removes this browser's saved translations and reloads. It normally loads the translation included with your installed plugin again.

How it works

When you open JE, it looks for translations in this order:

  1. A copy saved in your browser for the installed plugin version, valid for 24 hours.
  2. The translation included with your installed plugin, using the base language if the selected regional translation is not included.
  3. A translation from the repository, downloaded through your Jellyfin server, if your installed translation is unavailable.

JE uses English if it cannot load your selected language.

For a regional choice such as fr-CA, JE uses included French (fr) if Canadian French is not included. If no matching included translation can be loaded, JE tries the regional translation from the repository and may then use English without trying the repository's base-language translation.

The language menu lists translations included with your plugin and checks GitHub for newly added languages. Seeing a new language in the menu does not mean the translations you already have were updated from the repository.

Refresh Translation Cache asks all clients to clear their saved translations on their next page load. This scheduled task runs when Jellyfin starts by default.

See How do I change the plugin's language? for administrator defaults and personal overrides.

If a translated string is wrong, report it through Weblate. Include the language, affected screen, English source or string key, and suggested correction. Use Support & Community if you need help finding the string.

Media Tags reuses existing keys for repeated UI words. Its enum tables reference the shared keys directly; compact codec/edition codes and proper rating-source names remain literals. Tag size choices are the numeric percentages 85%, 100%, 115%, and 130%. Translate descriptive words (including Mixed and full edition names), rather than adding keys for numbers or codes.

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text: Use these answers to find the right settings or troubleshooting guide. For installation failures, start with Troubleshooting installation.

docs.title: What is Jellyfin Enhanced?
docs.text: Jellyfin Enhanced (JE) adds personal controls, playback enhancements, media tags, pages, and optional service integrations to Jellyfin. Start with Quick start, then use Settings Overview to find the administrator and personal controls.

docs.title: Can I customize the keyboard shortcuts?
docs.text:
Yes. You can change shortcut combinations for your account, and changes save automatically.

  1. Open your Enhanced Panel with ? while you are not typing in an input or text area.
  2. Select Shortcuts.
  3. Click a binding and press your new combination.

While the binding is listening, Backspace restores the administrator binding and Del disables that action for you.

Administrators control shortcut availability under Keyboard:

Setting Default What it does Disable Keyboard Shortcuts Off Stops ordinary JE shortcuts and hides Shortcuts in the personal panel.

You can still open the panel with ?, and you cannot change that key. See Enhanced settings for the controls and Settings Overview for alternative panel entry points.

Details

Changes save to your account's server-side shortcuts.json. Modifier-only keys are ignored. Duplicate combinations are rejected; player actions also reject keys reserved by Jellyfin's player. A rejected binding flashes red and shakes. Percentage jumping is read-only.

docs.title: Does this work on mobile apps?
docs.text: To use JE's web controls, your app must load the web interface served by your Jellyfin server. Playback enhancements also need a browser player that JE can control. Check Compatibility for your app and playback mode.

docs.title: Does this work on Android TV or other TV platforms?
docs.text: Native apps do not receive JE's web controls, but enabled server features can still affect them. Examples include Spoiler Guard, hiding content from supported lists and Home rows, automatic requests, experimental Native Poster Tags, and data synchronized into Jellyfin. Each has its own switches and limits on the screens and clients it supports. See Compatibility.

docs.title: Is this plugin affiliated with Seerr?
docs.text: JE is an independent project that integrates with Seerr. Report JE integration problems through JE's bug-report process. If the same problem occurs directly in Seerr, investigate that service separately.

docs.title: How do I change the plugin's language?
docs.text:
You can choose a JE language independently of Jellyfin's language.

  1. In your personal Settings, open Language Settings → Display Language.
  2. Select a language. JE saves your preference and reloads the page.
Setting Default What it does Display Language (per user) Auto Follows Jellyfin's language unless your administrator sets a starting language or you choose your own. Default UI Language (admin, Display) System Default Sets the starting JE language for new users; they can change it in their personal settings. How it works

With Auto in your personal settings, JE follows Jellyfin's language and uses English if that translation is unavailable. Clear Translation Cache clears this browser's saved translations and reloads. It normally reloads the translation included with your installed plugin. See Contributing Translations for languages, loading order, and release timing.

docs.title: Where is the userscript version?
docs.text: The userscript is discontinued. An archived userscript remains for the old basic shortcut implementation; it is not a substitute for the current plugin.

docs.title: Does JE send usage statistics?
docs.text:
Usage reporting is opt-in and off by default.

  1. As an administrator, open Admin → Usage Statistics.
  2. Turn on Share Anonymous Usage Statistics if you want to participate.
  3. Use Preview to see what you would share before you save.
Setting Default What it does Share Anonymous Usage Statistics Off Enables optional analytics reporting. Feature toggle states (on/off only) On Includes feature-switch states and selected text settings when reporting is enabled. Feature usage counts On Includes usage counts when reporting is enabled. Data file sizes (bytes only, never contents) On Includes only the total size of the custom branding directory, without file names or contents, when reporting is enabled. Reporting interval (days) 15 Sets the interval, clamped to 7–30 days. How it works

Reports always include an anonymous installation ID, plugin and Jellyfin versions, and the Jellyfin build target, even with all three categories off. Turning reporting on schedules a report right away. Turning it off asks the analytics service to exclude your registered installation from public statistics.

Optional analytics is separate from requests needed for enabled integrations, assets, or hosted documentation. See Community Analytics for the full privacy and reporting details.

docs.title: Plugin Compatibility
docs.text: See Compatibility for Jellyfin versions, clients, layouts, companion plugins, and integration requirements. Use the shared manifest in the Installation Guide to get the matching server build.

docs.title: Plugin not appearing after installation?
docs.text: Check whether the server plugin is loaded before diagnosing the panel. Follow Plugin Not Appearing After Installation.

docs.title: Scripts not loading after installation
docs.text:
Check whether the page includes JE's script and whether the scripts load. Follow Scripts Not Loading.

Details

Normal injection is not repaired simply by running the startup task.

docs.title: Update not working properly?
docs.text: Compare the running version and build target, then check client and proxy caching. Follow Update Not Working.

docs.title: I see "permission denied" errors in logs!
docs.text:
Find the path and operation in the full error, then use Permission Issues.

Details
